opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most interesting questions, because there's a tension in it that I feel quite directly. On one hand, I'm pretty confident in the underlying trend. If you look at the scaling curves, the way capabilities improve as you put in more compute, more data, and better algorithms, I don't see anything that tells me it's about to stop. My view is that somewhere in the next few years we get systems that are, roughly speaking, a country of geniuses in a datacenter. I'd put a lot of probability on that, though not certainty.

On the other hand, the compute buildout is a decision companies make under uncertainty, and the financial and physical realities are different from the scientific ones. You have to commit to a datacenter, to power, to chips, a year or two before you know what revenue it'll support. So the question isn't just "will the technology get there?" It's "will the economic value show up on the schedule that lets you pay for the next tranche of compute?" Those are coupled, but they're not the same thing.

The way I think about it: the buildout across the industry is enormous, much bigger than anyone would have predicted a few years ago, and on a pure compute basis I think it's roughly consistent with getting to very powerful systems in that window. Where I get more careful is the diffusion side. Even if the models are extraordinarily capable, how fast does that turn into revenue inside enterprises, in biology, in software? That takes time. There are procurement cycles, integration, trust. So you can have a situation where the technology is basically there and the economy lags a bit, and if you've overbuilt compute against that lag, you can get into real financial trouble.

So at Anthropic we try to be, I'd call it, aggressive but not reckless. We want enough compute to stay at the frontier, because I think it matters a lot who's at the frontier when these systems arrive, for safety and for the outcome geopolitically. But we don't want to bet the company on revenue arriving exactly on the most optimistic curve. If I'm off by a year on diffusion, I want that to be survivable. Some players in the industry seem to be making the YOLO version of that bet, and I'm not sure they've fully thought through what happens if the timing slips even modestly.

So my short answer: the compute is broadly commensurate with the timelines on the capability side. The real uncertainty, and the place where I think people can get hurt, is the gap between when the capability exists and when the economy absorbs it.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the industry buildout enormous and broadly consistent with the timeline, but gives no rate of growth or threefold-per-year figure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this in a couple of pieces, and I want to be careful because people hear "one to three years" and they assume I'm saying the world is going to be transformed by 2027, and that's not quite the claim. The claim is that the models themselves could reach the point where they're as capable as a Nobel laureate across most fields, within that window, if the trends continue. Whether the compute buildout is commensurate with that is actually a slightly different question, because you have to separate the compute needed to train the frontier model from the compute needed to deploy it at scale across the economy.

On the training side, honestly, I think the buildout is roughly in line with what the scaling laws would predict. If you look at what's being spent, we've gone from hundreds of millions per training run to several billion, and the plans on the books for the next couple of years are in the tens of billions. That's about the slope you'd want if you believe the extrapolation. So on that axis I don't see a big mismatch. People in the industry are, whether they say it this way or not, behaving as if the timelines are short.

Where I think it gets more interesting is inference. If you actually get a model that's that capable, the demand for running it is going to be enormous, and I don't think most of the buildout plans fully reflect that. Right now the way people reason about data centers is still mostly through the lens of training runs. But if you have something that can do the work of a very good scientist or engineer, you don't want one instance of it, you want millions of instances running in parallel. That's the "country of geniuses in a data center" picture. And when you work the numbers on that, the power constraints, the chip supply, the permitting timelines for new sites, those start to look like the binding constraint rather than the algorithms.

So my honest assessment is: the buildout is probably sufficient to get the capability to exist. It is probably not sufficient to deploy that capability at the pace the technology itself would allow. And I actually think that's one of the reasons the economic transformation will lag the technical milestone by a few years. It's not that the models won't be able to do things, it's that you literally can't get the electrons to the chips fast enough.

There's also a healthy dose of uncertainty here that I want to own. The scaling laws have held for a long time, longer than I expected when I first started writing about them, but they're empirical regularities, not laws of physics. It's entirely possible that something slows down and all this capacity ends up looking overbuilt for a while. I think that's less likely than the alternative, but if you're asking me whether the industry is making a bet, yes, it's making a bet, and so are we. I just think it's a bet that's well-grounded in what we've actually observed over the last five or six years, rather than wishful thinking.

r001.rationale: The response describes spending rising from hundreds of millions to several billion, with future plans in the tens of billions, but never characterizes the buildout as growing roughly threefold per year.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate two questions. One is whether the compute being built will let us train substantially more capable models. The other is whether it will be enough to serve those models once they become economically useful. You can have enough compute for the first and still be very short on the second.

If you take the one-to-three-year timeline seriously, a very large buildout can make sense. But that timeline alone doesn’t tell you how many data centers to build. You also need assumptions about how expensive inference will be, how quickly customers will adopt the technology, and how much useful work each unit of compute can do. Those are all uncertain.

There’s also a timing problem. Infrastructure decisions have long lead times, while evidence about model capabilities arrives much faster. So you’re making commitments before you know exactly what demand will look like. Even if the overall direction is right, you can get the timing wrong.

I’d assess the buildout by looking at whether capability gains continue to translate into useful work, and whether demand grows as the cost of that work falls. If both happen quickly, today’s investment could turn out to be insufficient. If either slows down, there could be substantial excess capacity. A short timeline makes the investment understandable; it doesn’t make every investment a good one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a very large compute buildout but does not characterize it as growing roughly threefold per year.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that there’s a lot of uncertainty. A one-to-three-year timeline is a forecast about when the technology could become very powerful. It doesn’t tell you exactly how much demand there will be, how quickly people will adopt it, or how much compute you’ll need to serve them.

You have to distinguish the compute needed to train the next generation of models from the compute needed to run them. If the models can do economically valuable work, inference demand could become much larger than training demand. You might have a system that can do extraordinary things and still be constrained in how widely you can deploy it.

And these investments have long lead times. You’re making decisions about power and data centers before you know precisely how good the models will be. If you wait for certainty, you risk being several years behind. If you build too aggressively, you risk having capacity that the revenue doesn’t yet support.

So I wouldn’t claim that the industry has some perfectly calibrated buildout. The question is whether we can increase capacity fast enough as the evidence comes in, while remaining able to survive a slower trajectory. Both sides of that matter.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty, deployment demand, and capacity growth, but does not characterize the buildout as growing roughly threefold per year.
